title: Sound and Beauty: Recitation, Calligraphy and the Inimitable
bigQuestion: Why have Muslims treated the sound and the written shape of the Qur'an as arts, and what does hearing or seeing the book add to reading it?

story.title: One Vowel, One Breath
story.kicker: In a packed hall, a reciter stretches a single sound until the room forgets to breathe.
paragraphs: The hall in Cairo holds several thousand people, and every seat is full. On the stage sits one man in a plain robe, with no microphone stand in front of him, only a small book open on a low table. He closes his eyes. He begins with the words Muslims say before reciting, asking protection from Satan, and then the opening formula, "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." His voice is low at first, almost a speaking voice.

Then he reaches a long vowel in the middle of an ayah, and he holds it. He does not hurry. The note rises a little, bends, and settles. Tajwid, the rules of recitation, tell him exactly how many counts a vowel like this may last. Within that rule he has freedom, and he uses all of it. The sound fills the room. Somewhere near the back a listener whispers "Allah," the traditional way of praising a beautiful phrase, and the whisper spreads.

When the breath ends, the silence is complete. Nobody claps. Clapping is not done for the Qur'an. The reciter takes a breath, repeats the same ayah in a different melodic mode, and the crowd leans forward, listening for what he will do with it this time. A listener who speaks no Arabic could still follow the shape of the sound: the rise, the pause, the return.

Muslims call this listening a form of worship, and they also call it an art. Reciters are known by name and by voice, the way singers are. Their recordings play in taxis, kitchens and mosques from Jakarta to Chicago. This chapter asks what it means for a book to be heard before it is read, and seen before it is understood. It begins with a claim the Qur'an makes about itself: that no one can produce anything like it.
story.think: The audience treats the reciter as an artist but does not applaud him. What does that tell you about how they understand the sound they are hearing?

lessons.title: The Challenge Verses
lessons.mainIdea: In several passages the Qur'an dares its doubters to produce something like it, and Muslims read these verses as the root of the doctrine of i'jaz, the book's inimitability.
reading: The Qur'an says a striking thing about itself. In Surah 2 (Al-Baqarah, The Cow), ayah 23, it addresses people who doubt that the book comes from God and tells them to produce one surah like it, calling on any helpers they wish. Surah 17 (Al-Isra, The Night Journey), ayah 88, widens the dare: even if all humans and *jinn* (unseen beings the Qur'an says God created from fire) joined together, they could not produce the like of this Qur'an. Similar passages appear in 10:38, 11:13 and 52:33–34. Scholars call these the *challenge* verses, in Arabic tahaddi.

Muslims read these verses as more than a boast. They became the seed of a doctrine called *i'jaz*, from an Arabic root meaning to make someone unable. The idea is that the Qur'an cannot be imitated, and that its inimitability is itself a sign that it comes from God. In the traditional account, the Prophet's Meccan opponents were master poets, and the fact that none of them met the challenge is treated as evidence. Muslims hold this as a matter of faith; historians describe it as a claim the text makes and a tradition built around it.

Notice what the challenge asks for and what it does not. It does not say the book is the longest or the oldest. It asks for something "like it," which leaves open the question of what the likeness would be. Is it the sound? The meaning? The knowledge in it? The arrangement of words? For a thousand years Muslim scholars have argued about exactly this, and their answers are the subject of the next lesson. For now the key point is that the Qur'an itself invites a comparison, and that invitation shaped how Muslims listen to it and look at it.

words.d: the Muslim doctrine that the Qur'an cannot be imitated; from an Arabic root meaning to render unable
passages such as 2:23 and 17:88 in which the Qur'an dares doubters to produce something like it
unseen beings that the Qur'an says God created from smokeless fire; they can believe or disbelieve, like humans

look.title: The Widest Dare
look.text: Say: Verily, though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like thereof though they were helpers one of another.
look.cite: Qur'an 17:88 (Al-Isra), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The verse does not say what "the like" would have to match. List three things a challenger might try to match, and say which you think the verse most likely means.

check.q: What do the challenge verses ask doubters to do?
choices: Translate the Qur'an into another language
Recite the Qur'an in a competition
check.why: Verses such as 2:23 and 17:88 dare doubters to produce a surah or a text like the Qur'an; that dare is the basis of i'jaz.

check.q: The term i'jaz comes from a root meaning what?
choices: To write in a straight line
check.why: I'jaz means inimitability; its root has the sense of rendering someone unable, here unable to match the book.

check.q: How does a historian describe i'jaz, as distinct from how a Muslim believer does?
choices: As a proven fact about all books
As a rule of Arabic grammar
As a claim the text makes and a tradition built around it
As a legal ruling of one law school
check.why: Muslims hold i'jaz as a matter of faith; a historian describes it as a claim the Qur'an makes and the doctrine that grew from it, without judging it.

lessons.title: How the Scholars Argued
lessons.mainIdea: Classical scholars gave different answers to what makes the Qur'an inimitable: its arrangement of words, its sound, its knowledge, or God's turning people away from trying.
reading: By the 900s the doctrine of i'jaz had a shelf of books devoted to it. Al-Baqillani (d. 1013), a theologian in Baghdad, wrote a work called I'jaz al-Qur'an. He compared the Qur'an with the most admired Arabic poems and argued that the book's language stood apart from every human style. Around the same time, al-Rummani and al-Khattabi wrote short treatises listing the features of Qur'anic speech. Their method was literary: they read the Qur'an the way a critic reads a poem, and then argued that no poet could have written it.

The most influential answer came from 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. c. 1078), a grammarian from Gorgan in Persia. In his book Dala'il al-I'jaz (The Proofs of Inimitability) he argued that the miracle lies in *nazm*, the arrangement of the words. Single words, he said, are shared by everyone; what no one could match is the way the Qur'an's words fit together so that each carries exactly the meaning the sentence needs. Later rhetoric in Arabic grew out of his ideas, and modern literary readers of the Qur'an still cite him.

Not every scholar agreed. Some early theologians of the *Mu'tazila* school, such as al-Nazzam (d. c. 845), proposed a different theory called *sarfa*, "turning away." On this view, humans could in principle write something like the Qur'an, but God turned their minds away from doing so. Most later scholars rejected sarfa, because it seemed to locate the miracle outside the text. Others pointed to the Qur'an's predictions, or to its knowledge of past prophets that an unlettered man in Mecca could not have had. These are Muslim arguments; a public-school class describes them and compares them rather than deciding among them.

words.d: arrangement; al-Jurjani's term for the way the Qur'an's words fit together, which he saw as the source of its inimitability
the theory, held by a few early theologians, that God turned people away from imitating the Qur'an
an early school of Muslim theology that stressed reason and God's justice; some of its members held the sarfa view

look.title: Three Answers to One Question
look.text: Three scholars are asked, "What exactly can no one imitate?" Al-Baqillani says: the style, which is unlike any poem or speech. Al-Jurjani says: the arrangement, the way each word sits in its sentence. Al-Nazzam says: nothing in the text itself; God simply turned people away from trying. All three accepted the doctrine of i'jaz.
look.prompt: Which of the three answers could a literary critic test by reading, and which could not? Explain how you decided.

check.q: Al-Jurjani located the Qur'an's inimitability in what?
choices: The arrangement of its words, nazm
check.why: In Dala'il al-I'jaz al-Jurjani argued that nazm, the arrangement of words in their sentences, is what no one can match.

check.q: What did the sarfa theory claim?
choices: God turned people away from imitating the Qur'an
The Qur'an's grammar cannot be learned
Only poets may recite the Qur'an
The Qur'an was revealed in every language
check.why: Sarfa, proposed by al-Nazzam of the Mu'tazila, held that people could have imitated the book but God turned their minds away; most later scholars rejected it.

check.q: Al-Baqillani's method was best described as what?
choices: Legal: comparing rulings of the law schools
Literary: comparing the Qur'an with admired Arabic poems
Musical: measuring the length of vowels
check.why: Al-Baqillani's I'jaz al-Qur'an set the Qur'an beside the most admired poems and argued that its language stood apart.

lessons.title: A Book Meant to Be Heard
lessons.mainIdea: The name Qur'an means recitation, and Muslim tradition says its first audience judged it by ear, which is why sound has always been part of its meaning.
reading: The word *Qur'an* comes from the Arabic root q-r-', to recite or read aloud. The first word Muslims believe was revealed, in Surah 96 (Al-'Alaq, The Clot), is from that same root: "Read," or "Recite." For its first twenty years the Qur'an existed mainly as sound. Muslims memorized it and recited it in prayer. Written notes on bone, leather and palm stalks were aids to memory, not a book. Tradition says the complete written copy, the *mushaf*, was gathered after the Prophet's death, and that the sound came first.

Arabic of the 600s was a culture of the ear. Tribes competed through poets, and audiences memorized long odes. The Qur'an entered that world, and its early listeners judged it, tradition says, by how it sounded. Its sentences often end in rhyme or near-rhyme, a pattern called *saj'*, and its short Meccan surahs move in quick, pulsing lines. Later Muslim scholars pointed to this sound as part of i'jaz. Modern scholars of Arabic literature, Muslim and not, describe the same features without deciding what they prove.

This is why, in Muslim practice, a person who has never studied Arabic can still be moved by the Qur'an. A Bosnian grandmother, a Nigerian schoolboy and an Indonesian shopkeeper all hear the same Arabic sounds in prayer. Each reads the meaning in a different language. Muslims say that a translation is not the Qur'an but an explanation of it, because the sound of the Arabic belongs to the revelation. For a student in a public school this is a fact about how the book is used. It explains why the rest of this chapter is about sound and sight as much as about words.

words.d: literally "recitation," from the Arabic root q-r-'; the name reflects the book's origin as spoken and heard words
a written copy of the Qur'an as a bound book; tradition says it was gathered after the Prophet's death
rhymed or near-rhymed prose; the Qur'an's verse endings often follow this pattern

look.title: The First Word
look.text: Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not.
look.cite: Qur'an 96:1–5 (Al-'Alaq), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The passage opens with "Read" and then praises "the pen." How do sound and writing both appear in these five lines?

check.q: What does the word Qur'an literally mean?
check.why: Qur'an comes from the root q-r-', to recite or read aloud; the name points to the book's spoken origin.

check.q: Why do Muslims say a translation is not the Qur'an?
choices: Translators are not allowed to be Muslims
The book may not leave Arabia
The sound of the Arabic is held to belong to the revelation
check.why: Muslims regard the Arabic sound as part of the revelation, so a translation counts as an explanation of the meaning rather than the Qur'an itself.

check.q: What is saj'?
choices: A written copy of the Qur'an
A melodic mode used by reciters
check.why: Saj' is rhymed prose; many of the Qur'an's verse endings follow this pattern, and scholars link it to how the book sounds.

lessons.title: Tajwid, the Rules of Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Tajwid is the set of rules for pronouncing the Qur'an, governing the length of vowels, nasal sounds and pauses, which reciters learn from a teacher by ear.
reading: Surah 73 (Al-Muzzammil, The Enshrouded One), ayah 4, tells the Prophet to recite the Qur'an slowly and in measure. From that command, Muslims developed *tajwid*, a word meaning to make good or beautiful. Tajwid is not a melody. It is a set of rules for pronouncing each letter from its correct point in the mouth and throat, for how long a vowel is stretched, and for where a reciter may pause. A reciter who sings beautifully but breaks these rules is judged to have recited badly.

The rules have names. *Madd* governs the lengthening of vowels: some are held for two counts, some for four or five, some for six. *Ghunnah* is a nasal hum on certain letters, held for about two counts. *Qalqalah* is a slight bounce given to five letters when they close a syllable. Idgham merges one letter into the next. A student learns these not from a chart but from a teacher, repeating an ayah until the teacher approves and gives an *ijazah*, a certificate that links the student in a chain of teachers reaching back, Muslims say, to the Prophet.

Because tajwid was passed on by ear, the written rules came later than the practice. Scholars in Baghdad and elsewhere wrote them down in the 900s and after; Ibn al-Jazari (d. 1429) composed a short poem of rules that students still memorize. Tajwid explains something the visitor at the beginning of this chapter noticed: the reciter held a vowel for exactly as long as the rule allowed and no longer. In Muslim understanding, beauty in recitation comes from obeying the rule precisely, not from escaping it.

words.d: the rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly, covering points of articulation, vowel length, nasal sounds and pauses
lengthening; the tajwid rules for how many counts a vowel is held
a nasal hum on certain letters, held for about two counts
a certificate from a teacher that a student may recite or teach, placing the student in a chain of teachers

look.title: How Long a Vowel Lasts
look.cite: Standard tajwid teaching for the Hafs reading; counts vary slightly by school
look.prompt: A reciter holds a natural madd for six counts. Would a tajwid teacher call that beautiful or wrong? Explain using the rules.

check.q: Which Qur'anic verse do Muslims cite as the basis for tajwid?
check.why: Surah 73:4 instructs the Prophet to recite slowly and in measure, and Muslims trace the discipline of tajwid to it.

check.q: What is an ijazah?
choices: A written copy of the Qur'an
A certificate linking a student to a chain of teachers
check.why: An ijazah is a teacher's certificate that a student may recite or teach, placing the student in a chain of transmission.

check.q: In Muslim understanding, where does beauty in recitation come from?
choices: From adding as many notes as possible
From reciting faster than other reciters
From reciting in the listener's own language
From following the rules of pronunciation precisely
check.why: Tajwid teaches that a beautiful recitation is one that keeps every rule of articulation and length; breaking a rule is judged a fault however fine the voice.

lessons.title: The Readings: Hafs and Warsh
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an is recited in several accepted readings, the qira'at, that differ in small points of pronunciation and wording; two of them are heard most widely today.
reading: Listen to a recording from Cairo and one from Morocco and you will hear small differences: a vowel that is long in one and short in the other, a word pronounced with a slight variation. These are the *qira'at*, the accepted readings. Muslim tradition holds that the Prophet recited the Qur'an in more than one way and that his companions carried these ways to the cities they settled. In Baghdad in the early 900s the scholar Ibn Mujahid (d. 936) selected seven readings as authoritative, each named after a master reciter of the 700s. Later scholars accepted three more, making ten.

Each reading is transmitted through two named students of its master, so a full name looks like "Hafs from 'Asim" or "Warsh from Nafi'." The reading of *Hafs* from 'Asim of Kufa became the basis of the Cairo edition printed in 1924. It is the one heard across most of the Muslim world today. The reading of *Warsh* from Nafi' of Medina is common in North and West Africa. The differences are real but limited: pronunciation, some vowels, a few word endings. Muslim scholars say the readings all go back to the Prophet. Historians study them as evidence of how the text was transmitted by voice.

Why does this matter for an art chapter? Because a reciter chooses a reading the way a musician chooses an instrument. Some master reciters are famous for performing the same passage in several readings in one sitting, and listeners who know the readings hear the shift. It also matters for study. When two printed Qur'ans seem to disagree on a word, the answer is often that they follow different readings. A careful student names the reading, just as a careful student names the translation.

words.d: the accepted readings of the Qur'an, seven or ten in number, differing in small points of pronunciation and wording
the transmission of the reading of 'Asim of Kufa; the most widely used reading today and the basis of the 1924 Cairo edition
the transmission of the reading of Nafi' of Medina; common in North and West Africa

look.title: Counting the Readings
rows: Year of the Cairo edition in the Hafs reading
look.cite: Standard accounts of the qira'at; Ibn Mujahid, Kitab al-Sab'a; Cairo edition 1924
look.prompt: If each of the ten readings has two transmitters, how many transmission names does a student have to learn? Why might a tradition keep such careful records?

check.q: Who selected seven readings as authoritative in the early 900s?
check.why: Ibn Mujahid of Baghdad (d. 936) chose seven readings, each named after a master reciter; later scholars added three.

check.q: Which reading is the basis of the 1924 Cairo edition?
check.why: The Cairo edition of 1924 follows the Hafs transmission of 'Asim's reading, which is now the most widely used.

check.q: The differences among the qira'at are mainly in what?
choices: Pronunciation, some vowels and a few word endings
check.why: The readings share the same surahs in the same order; they differ in limited points of pronunciation and wording.

lessons.title: Murattal and Mujawwad
lessons.mainIdea: Reciters perform in two main styles, the measured murattal and the slow, ornamented mujawwad, and the great Egyptian reciters of the twentieth century made both famous through radio and recordings.
reading: Two words describe how the Qur'an is performed. *Murattal* is measured recitation: steady, clear, at a reading pace, the style used in daily prayer and in teaching. *Mujawwad* is slow, melodic and ornamented, the style of the concert hall and the radio broadcast, in which a reciter may repeat an ayah several times, exploring it in different melodic modes. Both follow tajwid. The difference is in pace and ornament, not in rules. A third term, hadr, names quick recitation used for review.

Twentieth-century Egypt produced the reciters whose voices define these styles for most Muslims. Mohamed Siddiq El-Minshawi (1920–1969) was known for a grave, sorrowful tone. Mahmoud Khalil al-Husary (1917–1980) was chosen to record the complete Qur'an in murattal, a recording used for teaching around the world. Abdul Basit Abdus-Samad (1927–1988) had a voice of unusual range and was invited to recite in mosques across the Muslim world; his mujawwad recordings remain among the most played. Mustafa Ismail (1905–1978) was admired for daring melodic choices. Egyptian state radio, which began broadcasting recitation in the 1930s, carried their voices far beyond Cairo.

Mujawwad reciters draw on the *maqam* system, the melodic modes of Arabic music, with names such as Bayati, Rast, Hijaz and Saba. A reciter does not sing in the sense of following a written tune; he improvises within a mode, matching its mood to the meaning of the verse. Muslim scholars have long debated how much melody is proper. Most accept it within the bounds of tajwid; some warn against turning the Qur'an into entertainment. Music historians study these recitations as one of the great vocal traditions of the world, while noting that reciters themselves usually do not call it music.

words.d: measured recitation at a steady reading pace, used in prayer and teaching
slow, melodic, ornamented recitation performed for listeners, following tajwid but exploring melody
a melodic mode in Arabic music, such as Bayati or Hijaz, within which a reciter improvises

look.title: Four Egyptian Voices
look.cite: Standard biographies of the Egyptian reciters; Egyptian radio broadcast recitation from the 1930s
look.prompt: All four were born within about twenty years of one another and all became famous through radio and records. What does that suggest about the role of new technology in this old art?

check.q: Which style is slow, ornamented and performed for listeners?
check.why: Mujawwad is the melodic, ornamented style of public recitation; murattal is the measured style of prayer and teaching.

check.q: Which reciter was chosen to record the complete Qur'an in murattal for teaching?
check.why: Al-Husary's complete murattal recording became a standard teaching recording; Ibn Mujahid lived a thousand years earlier.

check.q: What is a maqam?
choices: A melodic mode in Arabic music
A written copy of the Qur'an
check.why: Maqamat are the melodic modes, such as Bayati and Hijaz, within which a mujawwad reciter improvises.

lessons.title: Competitions and the Hafiz
lessons.mainIdea: International recitation competitions, held since the 1960s, honor young hafiz who have memorized the whole Qur'an, and they show how memory, tajwid and voice are judged together.
reading: A *hafiz* (feminine hafiza) is a person who has memorized the entire Qur'an, about 6,200 ayahs, and can recite any passage on request. Muslim tradition honors the hafiz because memory was the first way the book was preserved. Many children begin memorizing at five or six and finish by their early teens; others complete it as adults. Memorization is taught by repetition with a teacher, a page or a few lines a day, with constant review so that older passages do not fade.

In the twentieth century, states began to hold competitions. Malaysia's international recitation competition in Kuala Lumpur dates from 1961 and is among the oldest. Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Iran, Turkey and Dubai (whose international award began in 1997) hold others, and competitors travel from dozens of countries. Judges score memory, tajwid, voice and the handling of pauses. A judge may stop a reciter mid-verse and ask for a passage from another part of the book. Prizes can be large, and winners become known at home. The 2011 documentary Koran by Heart followed three ten-year-olds at the Cairo competition, including a girl from the Maldives and a boy from Tajikistan who knew little Arabic beyond the text he had memorized.

The competitions raise a question that Muslims themselves discuss. Is recitation a performance to be scored, or an act of worship that should not be? Supporters say the events encourage children and preserve tajwid. Critics worry that prizes and cameras change the purpose. A student in a public school does not need to settle that debate; the point is to see how a religious community argues about its own art. Chicago's Muslim communities hold local competitions in the same spirit, and many mosques in the area run memorization classes for children.

words.d: a person who has memorized the entire Qur'an; the feminine form is hafiza
learning the Qur'an by heart through daily repetition and review with a teacher
a judged public event in which reciters are scored on memory, tajwid, voice and pauses

look.title: The Judge's Interruption
look.text: A ten-year-old competitor is reciting Surah 19 (Maryam) when a judge raps the table and says the first words of an ayah from Surah 36 (Ya Sin). The boy must find the place in memory and continue from there without a pause. He does. The hall murmurs approval. Later he says he does not understand most of the Arabic he recites, though he plans to study it.
look.prompt: What does the interruption test that a straight recitation would not? What is gained, and what is not yet gained, by memorizing a text before understanding it?

check.q: What is a hafiz?
choices: A reciter who wins a competition
A person who has memorized the whole Qur'an
A judge at a recitation contest
check.why: A hafiz has memorized the entire Qur'an and can recite any passage; competitions honor such people but the title does not depend on winning.

check.q: Which country's international recitation competition dates from 1961?
check.why: Malaysia's competition in Kuala Lumpur began in 1961; Dubai's international award began in 1997.

check.q: What debate among Muslims do the competitions raise?
choices: Whether the Qur'an should be memorized at all
Whether recitation should be scored as a performance
check.why: Supporters say competitions encourage children and preserve tajwid; critics worry that prizes and cameras change worship into performance.

lessons.title: From Hijazi to Kufic
lessons.mainIdea: The earliest Qur'an manuscripts use a slanting script called Hijazi and then the angular Kufic, written on parchment, and they show the book becoming a visual object.
reading: The oldest surviving Qur'an leaves are written on *parchment*, prepared animal skin, in a tall, slanting script that scholars call *Hijazi*, after the region of Mecca and Medina. The letters lean to the right, the lines are uneven, and there are few marks for short vowels. Two such leaves in the University of Birmingham library were radiocarbon-dated in 2015 to between about 568 and 645 CE with high probability. The dating is of the skin, not the ink. Scholars debate how soon after preparation the writing was done. Still, the leaves are among the earliest witnesses to the text.

By the 700s a new script took over: *Kufic*, named after the city of Kufa in Iraq, though it was used far more widely. Kufic is angular and horizontal. Its letters stretch along the line, its verticals are short, and its pages are often wider than they are tall. Scribes ruled the parchment carefully and placed a fixed number of lines on each page, so that a Kufic Qur'an looks as ordered as a building. Red dots marked vowels; gold rosettes marked the ends of verses. The text now had a visual rhythm to match its spoken one.

The most famous Kufic manuscript is the *Blue Qur'an*, made around the 800s or 900s, probably in North Africa. Its pages are dyed deep indigo and its Kufic letters are written in gold, fifteen lines to a page. Only scattered leaves survive, in museums from Tunis to New York. No one is sure who ordered it; some scholars link it to the Fatimid court, others to earlier rulers. What is certain is that by then the written Qur'an had become a work of art, made to be seen as well as read, and that its beauty was meant to honor the words rather than decorate them.

words.d: prepared animal skin used for writing before paper became common in the Muslim world
the slanting script of the earliest Qur'an manuscripts, named after the region of Mecca and Medina
an angular, horizontal script used for Qur'ans from the 700s to the 900s and beyond
a famous Kufic manuscript in gold letters on indigo parchment, made around the 800s or 900s in North Africa

look.title: Dating the Earliest Scripts
rows: Kufic script in wide use, from about (CE)
look.cite: University of Birmingham announcement, 2015; standard surveys of Islamic calligraphy
look.prompt: The radiocarbon date is for the parchment. Why is that not the same as a date for the writing, and what else would a historian want to know?

check.q: What does the 2015 radiocarbon date of the Birmingham leaves measure?
choices: The age of the vowel marks
check.why: Radiocarbon dating tested the animal skin; the ink cannot be dated that way, so scholars discuss how soon the writing followed.

check.q: Kufic script is best described as what?
choices: Tiny and used only for notes
check.why: Kufic letters stretch along the line with short verticals; Hijazi is the slanting early script.

check.q: What makes the Blue Qur'an unusual to look at?
choices: It has pictures of the prophets
It is written in Latin letters
Each page holds only one word
check.why: The Blue Qur'an's pages are dyed indigo and written in gold Kufic; Qur'ans do not include pictures of prophets.

lessons.title: The Six Pens
lessons.mainIdea: From the 900s calligraphers developed rounded scripts governed by proportion, and Naskh, Thuluth and their relatives became the standard hands of the Qur'an for the next thousand years.
reading: In Baghdad in the early 900s a vizier and calligrapher named Ibn Muqla (d. 940) worked out a system of *proportion* for Arabic letters. Every letter was measured against the diamond-shaped dot made by the pen's tip and the height of the letter alif. With this system, rounded scripts could be as disciplined as Kufic. A generation later Ibn al-Bawwab (d. 1022) refined the method, and a Qur'an he copied in Baghdad in the year 1000 or 1001, now in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin, is the earliest surviving complete Qur'an in the rounded *Naskh* script.

Naskh, whose name means "copying," is clear, even and quick to write. It became the everyday script of Qur'ans and remains the model for printed Arabic. *Thuluth*, meaning "one third," is larger and more sweeping, with tall verticals and deep curves, and it is used for headings and for inscriptions on buildings. Together with Muhaqqaq, Rayhan, Tawqi' and Riqa', these make up the *Six Pens*, the classical rounded scripts, which the calligrapher Yaqut al-Musta'simi (d. 1298) is credited with perfecting in Baghdad. Other regions kept their own hands: Maghribi in North Africa and Spain, with its rounded loops below the line, and Bihari in India.

The Ottoman Turks made calligraphy a court art. Sheikh Hamdullah (d. 1520) set the Ottoman style of Naskh, and Hafiz Osman (d. 1698) copied Qur'ans that later scribes imitated for centuries. A calligrapher trained for years under a master and, like a reciter, received an ijazah before signing work. The finest mushafs were also *illuminated*: the opening pages framed in gold and lapis blue, verse markers picked out in color, surah titles in gold on ornamented panels. Figures of people and animals never appear in a Qur'an; the art is the letter itself. In 2021 UNESCO placed Arabic calligraphy on its list of intangible cultural heritage.

words.d: Ibn Muqla's system for measuring each letter against the pen's dot and the height of alif
the clear, rounded script that became the everyday hand of the Qur'an and the model for printed Arabic; the name means copying
a large, sweeping rounded script used for headings and inscriptions on buildings
the six classical rounded scripts: Naskh, Thuluth, Muhaqqaq, Rayhan, Tawqi' and Riqa'
decorated with gold and colored ornament, especially on the opening pages and verse markers

look.title: Masters of the Pen
look.cite: Standard surveys of Islamic calligraphy; Chester Beatty Library, Ibn al-Bawwab Qur'an of 1000–1001
look.prompt: Place these five men on a line and mark the cities Baghdad and Istanbul. What does the sequence tell you about where the center of this art moved over time?

check.q: What did Ibn Muqla contribute to calligraphy?
choices: A system of proportion for letters
check.why: Ibn Muqla (d. 940) measured letters against the pen's dot and the height of alif; Sheikh Hamdullah set the Ottoman Naskh style much later.

check.q: Which script is large and sweeping and used for inscriptions on buildings?
check.why: Thuluth, with its tall verticals and deep curves, is the script of headings and architectural bands; Naskh is the everyday copying hand.

check.q: What never appears in an illuminated Qur'an?
check.why: Qur'an illumination uses gold, color and pattern; figures of people and animals are not drawn in a mushaf.

lessons.title: The Qur'an on Buildings
lessons.mainIdea: Since the 600s Muslims have written Qur'anic verses on mosques, shrines and tombs, so that the walls themselves speak the text to anyone who can read them.
reading: Walk into almost any mosque and you will see writing where a church might have pictures. Bands of Thuluth run around the base of the dome; Kufic frames the doorway; a roundel over the prayer niche carries a single verse. The choice of verse is deliberate. The Throne Verse (2:255) is common because it speaks of God's power and care. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas, Sincerity), which declares God's oneness, appears on countless walls. The Light Verse (24:35) often surrounds a lamp or a window, since it compares God's light to a lamp in a niche.

The oldest surviving example is the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed in 691 or 692 under the Umayyad caliph 'Abd al-Malik. A mosaic inscription about 240 meters long runs around the inner arcade. It includes Surah 112 and passages about Jesus ('Isa) such as 4:171. Historians note that these were addressed to the largely Christian city around it. The Taj Mahal in Agra, built in the 1630s and 1640s, carries whole surahs in black stone inlaid into white marble. They include Surah 36 (Ya Sin), often recited for the dead. The calligrapher Amanat Khan signed his work on the building. Each year a new *kiswa*, the black cloth covering the Kaaba in Mecca, is embroidered with verses in gold and silver thread.

Historians read these inscriptions as evidence. A verse chosen for a building tells what its patron wanted said and to whom, and the script tells the date and region. Art historians also note that Qur'anic writing on buildings is rarely placed where it can be read easily; a band under a dome is far above the eye. The writing works as presence as much as message. Muslims say the text sanctifies the space. A visitor to one of Chicago's mosques can see the same tradition in newer form: Thuluth bands over the prayer hall, often made by calligraphers trained in Turkey, Egypt or Pakistan.

words.d: writing carved, painted or set in mosaic on a building
the black cloth covering the Kaaba in Mecca, embroidered each year with Qur'anic verses
a shrine in Jerusalem completed in 691 or 692, carrying the oldest surviving Qur'anic inscriptions on a building

look.title: A Verse for a Wall
look.text: Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him.
look.cite: Qur'an 112:1–4 (Al-Ikhlas), trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: This surah is inscribed on the Dome of the Rock in a city that was then mostly Christian. Why might a ruler choose these four lines for that place, according to historians?

choices: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem
check.why: The Dome of the Rock, completed in 691 or 692, has a long mosaic inscription that includes Surah 112 and verses on Jesus.

check.q: What is the kiswa?
choices: The prayer niche in a mosque
The cloth covering the Kaaba, embroidered with verses
check.why: The kiswa is the black cloth over the Kaaba, renewed each year and embroidered with Qur'anic verses.

check.q: Why do art historians say the writing under a dome works as presence more than message?
choices: Because it is written in a secret code
Because it is too high to read easily

check.why: Bands of script under a dome sit far above the eye; historians note they sanctify the space even when they cannot be read.

lessons.title: The Qur'an in Poetry
lessons.mainIdea: Persian poets such as Rumi and Hafez wove Qur'anic verses into their poems, and through them the Qur'an reached readers far outside the mosque, including Goethe in Germany.
reading: Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207–1273), a scholar and Sufi teacher who lived in Konya in what is now Turkey, wrote a vast Persian poem called the Masnavi. It is made of stories, some funny, some strange. Nearly every one turns on a Qur'anic verse. Rumi quotes the Arabic, then unfolds it in Persian. A later Persian poet is often credited with calling the Masnavi "the Qur'an in the Persian tongue." Rumi himself, in the *Sufi* way, read the Qur'an as having layers. There is an outer meaning for everyone and inner meanings for those who search.

Hafez of Shiraz (d. c. 1390) took his pen name from the word *hafiz*; in his own verses he says he knew the Qur'an by heart. His ghazals, short lyric poems about wine, love and the beloved, are read by Muslims in at least two ways. Some hear them as songs about earthly love and pleasure. Others hear the wine as a symbol of God's love, in the Sufi manner. Iranian families keep a volume of Hafez beside the Qur'an and open it for guidance, a practice called fal-e Hafez. The debate over how to read him mirrors the debate over how to read the Qur'an itself: literally, or for a hidden sense.

In 1819 the German poet Goethe published the West-östlicher Divan, a book of poems written in answer to Hafez, whom he had read in translation. Goethe also read the Qur'an in German and Latin versions. He copied out passages in his notebooks. Through Hafez and Goethe, Qur'anic ideas traveled into world literature. Later, translations of Rumi became bestsellers in the United States. A student reading Rumi in English today may not notice that a line is a verse of the Qur'an. Part of the work of this course is to learn to hear it.

words.d: a Muslim who follows the mystical path of Islam, seeking closeness to God; Sufi readers often find inner meanings in the Qur'an
Rumi's long Persian poem of stories built on Qur'anic verses, written in the 1200s
a short lyric poem, often about love, in the Persian and Arabic traditions

look.title: Wine or Love of God?
look.text: A ghazal of Hafez praises wine, the tavern and a beloved whose face outshines the moon. One reader says: this is a poem about a night of pleasure in Shiraz. Another says: the wine is God's love, the tavern is the Sufi lodge, and the beloved is God. Hafez signed the poem with a name that means "one who has memorized the Qur'an."
look.prompt: What evidence inside and outside the poem could support each reading? How is this like the debate over reading a verse of the Qur'an for its outer or inner meaning?

check.q: What is the Masnavi?
choices: A book of Persian ghazals by Hafez
Rumi's long Persian poem built on Qur'anic verses
check.why: Rumi's Masnavi tells stories that unfold Qur'anic verses; Hafez wrote ghazals, and al-Tabari wrote a tafsir.

check.q: Hafez's pen name comes from what word?
choices: Hafiz, one who has memorized the Qur'an
Hafs, a transmitter of a reading
check.why: Hafez took his name from hafiz; he says in his poems that he knew the Qur'an by heart.

check.q: Which German poet answered Hafez with a book of poems in 1819?
check.why: Goethe's West-östlicher Divan (1819) was written in response to Hafez, whom he read in translation.

lessons.title: Fiction, Film and the Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Novelists and filmmakers have brought the Qur'an to audiences who may never open it, while working within Muslim reluctance to show the Prophet.
reading: The best-known film about the Qur'an's origins is The Message, released in 1976 and directed by Moustapha Akkad, a Syrian-born filmmaker who worked in Hollywood. It tells the story of Muhammad's mission from the first revelation to the return to Mecca. Following long Muslim custom, the Prophet is never shown or heard; the camera takes his point of view, and other characters speak to him. Akkad shot the film twice, once with an English-speaking cast and once with an Arabic one. Some Muslim authorities objected before release; today the film is widely shown in Muslim countries.

Documentaries have taken a different route, filming the Qur'an's readers rather than its story. Koran by Heart (2011) followed children at the Cairo recitation competition. Other films have recorded calligraphers at work and reciters in performance. Novelists, too, have written about people who live with the book. Leila Aboulela, born in Sudan, writes in English about Muslim characters whose faith is part of ordinary life; her novel The Translator (1999) is one example. Mohja Kahf's The Girl in the Tangerine Scarf (2006) follows a Syrian American girl growing up in Indiana, with Qur'anic verses woven into her story.

These works matter for a student of the Qur'an because they show reception: how the text lives in the minds of readers. They also show limits. A film cannot recite for you; a novel cannot show calligraphy. And both filmmakers and novelists must decide how to handle a text that many of their audience hold sacred. Some avoid quoting it, some quote it reverently, and a few use it critically. Reading how each artist made that choice is itself a way of studying the Qur'an's place in the world.

words.d: how a text has been received, read and used by later audiences, including artists
a 1976 film by Moustapha Akkad on the origins of Islam, in which the Prophet is never shown
a nonfiction film; several have recorded reciters, calligraphers and competitions

look.title: Filming a Prophet Without Showing Him
look.text: In The Message, when other characters speak to Muhammad, they look straight into the camera. When he rides, we see the camel from his saddle. When he speaks, the audience hears only the reply. The director said he wanted Muslims to be able to watch the film without offense, and non-Muslims to learn the story.
look.prompt: What does this technique gain and lose for a viewer? How does it reflect a tradition that expresses reverence through writing rather than pictures?

check.why: Following Muslim custom, Akkad's film never shows or voices the Prophet; the camera takes his point of view.

choices: The room where guests are greeted at a mosque

check.why: Reception is the study of how a text has been read and used by later audiences, including novelists and filmmakers.

lessons.title: Listening and Looking as Reading
lessons.mainIdea: For Muslims, hearing the Qur'an recited and seeing it written are ways of receiving the text, and a student can learn to notice what each way adds to reading for meaning.
reading: This chapter has moved from sound to script to poetry and film. One idea runs through all of it. In Muslim practice, the Qur'an is not only read for information; it is heard, seen, memorized and inscribed. A hadith recorded by Abu Dawud has the Prophet tell his followers to beautify the Qur'an with their voices, and another, in al-Bukhari's collection, praises the person who learns the Qur'an and teaches it. Sufi writers speak of *sama'*, listening, as a discipline of the heart. Muslims describe these as ways of drawing near to the text; historians describe them as ways a community has kept a text alive for fourteen centuries.

A student can borrow the habit without borrowing the belief. Listening to a recording of Surah 1 in the Hafs reading, even without Arabic, teaches you where the pauses fall and which sounds repeat. Looking at a Kufic page teaches you how early readers divided verses and marked vowels. Comparing a Thuluth inscription with the printed text shows which verses a community chose to display. None of this replaces reading the words in translation. It adds *context*: the setting in which the words have been received.

This is also good practice for the capstone that follows. When you choose a verse to study, you will ask what it says, but also how it sounds in recitation, where it has been inscribed, and which poets or artists have taken it up. Those are all forms of *evidence* about how a text has been read. The habit of asking them transfers to any text you will meet: a poem, a speech, a law. Sound and beauty are not a distraction from meaning. In this tradition, Muslims would say, they are part of it.

words.d: listening; in Sufi thought, attentive hearing of recitation or sacred song as a spiritual discipline
the setting in which a text is received: its sound, its script, its place and its readers
facts, such as a recording, a manuscript or an inscription, that support a claim about how a text has been read

look.title: Beautify It With Your Voices
look.text: In a report preserved in the collection of Abu Dawud, the Prophet is said to have told his followers to make the Qur'an beautiful with their voices. Muslim scholars have cited this saying for centuries to explain why melodic recitation is encouraged, while also warning that the rules of tajwid must not be broken for the sake of melody.

It names the city of Jerusalem

review.why: Al-Ikhlas states tawhid, God's oneness, briefly and clearly, which made it a favorite for walls from the Dome of the Rock onward.
